hook_stories.text: Imagine you're on a field trip to a local science center in Toronto. You enter a large room where there are hundreds of tiny, glowing creatures moving under a microscope. The guide tells you about **cells**, the basic units of life. As you watch, a fish scale falls on the floor near you. The teacher says, “You know what? That scale had cells — and every time you scratch your knee, you’re dealing with the **repairs** of your own cells.” Suddenly, an alarm rings, and everyone is asked to head to a greenhouse nearby. When you're inside, the guide points to a red maple leaf (a common Canadian tree). “This leaf contains hundreds of **plant cells** – and each cell has special features that help it live.” She tells you that **chloroplasts** inside the leaf help the tree make food using sunlight – just like the solar panels on your home. You look closely and realize that even the **tiniest organisms**, like bacteria or yeast in the soil, are made of **cells** – and they're alive too. This is the world of **cells**.
hook_stories.closing_line: This is the world of cells.

explanation_steps: A cell is the basic building block of all living things. Living things can be made of just one cell, or trillions of cells.
There are two types of organisms: unicellular (one cell) like paramecium or yeast, and multicellular (many cells) like humans and trees.
Plant cells have features in addition to those of animal cells: a cell wall that protects and gives shape, and chloroplasts that make food using sunlight.

Organelles have specific functions: the nucleus controls cell activities, mitochondria make energy for the cell, the cell wall supports and protects plant cells, and chloroplasts make food for plant cells using sunlight.
Cells help us grow, heal, and function. When you get a cut, your body uses cells to heal and repair it. When you eat food, your cells break it down and use it for energy and growth.
concept.whiteboard_text: Cell = Basic Unit of Life. Animal: Nucleus, Mitochondria. Plant: Nucleus, Mitochondria, Cell Wall, Chloroplast.
concept.comprehension_check: Which of the following best describes what a cell is?
reteach_angles: If we think of a building, the blocks that make up the building are like the cells in our body.
Think about a garden – every plant in the garden is made of tiny building blocks called cells.

problems.text: Lila is looking at a leaf under her microscope. She sees a structure in the cell that allows the plant to make food from sunlight. What is this structure?
problems.answer_explanation: Chloroplasts are found in plant cells and use sunlight to make food (glucose) from carbon dioxide and water. This is called photosynthesis.
problems.common_misconception: Students might confuse the function of chloroplasts with that of mitochondria, thinking chloroplasts make energy.

intervention_hints.level_1: What part of the plant cell makes light into food?
intervention_hints.level_2: The chloroplast is like a kitchen – what does it use?
intervention_hints.level_3: If a leaf were a solar-powered house, what part would catch the sun’s light and turn it into food?

problems.text: Which of the following is TRUE about both plant and animal cells?
problems.answer: C. They both have a nucleus
problems.answer_explanation: The nucleus is found in all living cells (both plant and animal) and holds the DNA that controls cell activities.
mc_choices: C. They both have a nucleus
B. They both have a cell wall
D. Only animal cells have mitochondria
problems.common_misconception: Students might think that chloroplasts are found in both plant and animal cells, or assume that only animal cells have mitochondria.

intervention_hints.level_1: What part is in ALL cells?
intervention_hints.level_2: The nucleus is like the brain – where is it in both types of cells?
intervention_hints.level_3: If a plant and animal are made of cells, which part must they both have?

problems.text: A student is comparing a cell from a mushroom (a fungus) with a cell from a maple tree. Which structure will be found in BOTH?
problems.answer_explanation: Every cell, whether from a tree or a mushroom, has a nucleus to store DNA and control cell activities.
problems.common_misconception: Students may incorrectly believe that all types of cells contain chloroplasts or cell walls.

intervention_hints.level_1: Fungi and plants are both living things – what do they always have?
intervention_hints.level_2: What makes the cell work and give energy?
intervention_hints.level_3: How can we tell that they’re both made of cells if one is a mushroom and the other is a tree?

problems.text: A student is studying two organisms. One is made of just one cell (like an amoeba), and one is made of many cells (like a maple tree). What are they both made of?
problems.answer: C. Both are made of cells
problems.answer_explanation: All living things are made of cells, whether it's a single-celled organism like an amoeba or a multicellular organism like a tree.
mc_choices: C. Both are made of cells
A. Both are made of bacteria cells
B. Both are made of animal cells
D. Both are made of plant cells
problems.common_misconception: Students may confuse how cells work in one type of organism with another or assume they must be identical unless stated otherwise.

intervention_hints.level_1: How are these two organisms alike?
intervention_hints.level_2: Think about the fish scale and a leaf – what do they have in common?
intervention_hints.level_3: Are there any other living things you've learned about that fit this description of being made of cells?

problems.text: A student is studying two organisms. One is made of just one cell (like an amoeba), and one is made of many cells (like a maple tree). What are they both made of? Two parts to the question: 1. How are they similar? 2. What is one way they are different?
problems.answer: 1. C. Both are made of cells. 2. One is unicellular, one is multicellular.
problems.answer_explanation: Both organisms are made of cells – this is the definition of a cell. One organism has cells that form one structure, and the other organism has many cells working together in different ways.
mc_choices: C. Both are made of cells
A. Both are made of bacteria cells
B. Both are made of animal cells
D. Both are made of plant cells
problems.common_misconception: Students might think that one organism is made of one type of cell while the other is made of another type.

intervention_hints.level_1: Think back to the fish scale and the leaf. How were they different, and how were they similar?
intervention_hints.level_2: What is the basic building block of all living things?
intervention_hints.level_3: If we compare an amoeba and a tree, both are living. What do they each have in common?

problems.nova_guiding_question: Think back to the fish scale and the leaf. How were they different, and how were they similar?

problems.text: Luis draws a diagram of a plant and an animal cell. What part should he include in BOTH types of cells?
problems.answer_explanation: The nucleus is found in all cells (plant, animal, fungal, bacterial), where it controls the activities and stores genetic information.
problems.common_misconception: Some students might believe that only plant cells contain chloroplasts or that only animal cells contain mitochondria.

intervention_hints.level_1: Are all cells the same inside or are there key differences?
intervention_hints.level_3: If you look at a diagram of plant and animal cells, which feature do they both share?
